newsitem.title: THAILAND: New Thai finmin faces first test in parliament.
newsitem.headline: New Thai finmin faces first test in parliament.

text.p: Thailand's new Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya will face a parliamentary grilling on the country's 1998 budget on Wednesday in his first test at the helm of Thailand's economic crisis.
Analysts said Thanong will encounter heavy pressure to explain Thailand's budget deficit this year, the first such shortfall after nine straight years of fiscal surplus.
The Budget Bureau last month estimated the Thai government's budget deficit for this year at 63.2 billion baht ($2.5 billion).

"The government will have to explain the situation clearly and for minister Thanong it will be his first experience on the budget at a critical time," said an analyst at a foreign brokerage who declined to be identified.
The battered economy is in its worst crisis since the early 1980s, squeezed by an unstable local currency, weak finance and property sectors, and a slumping stock market.

It will be Thanong's first step into political debate over the economy since the low-profile banker last week replaced widely respected Amnuay Viravan who quit following differences with his rivals in government.

The opposition, led by the Democrat Party, has said it would focus in the three-day budget debate on challenging the government's plan to resume its policy of adopting balanced, deficit-free budgets after a brief disruption this year.
The finance ministry says the economic slowdown has cut heavily into the government's tax revenue since mid-1996, a situation it expects to continue into 1998.
Amnuay, before his resignation, won cabinet approval last month for a 26.59 billion baht budget cut which would trim the proposed 1997/98 (October/September) government spending to 982 billion baht.
He said the cut would help spare the government a second budget deficit two years in a row.

The austerity budget next year represents a small four percent increase from the government's estimated 1996/97 expenditure of 944 billion baht, also the smallest year-on-year growth in more than a decade.

But Abhisit Vejjajiva, spokesman of the Democrat Party, said Amnuay under-estimated the government revenue loss and his budget cut was too small to help the country avoid another hefty deficit next year.

Finance permanent secretary Chatumonkol Sonakul said on Monday the government would seek an additional 16 billion baht revenue contribution by state enterprises next year to help balance the new budget.
Government spokesman Varathep Rattanakorn said the 1997/98 proposed budget reflected government efforts to maintain economic stability without choking off development growth.
Analysts said despite the change of finance minister, Prime Minister Chavalit Yonchaiyudh's six-party coalition expects an easy passage of the budget during its first reading in parliament this week.
The coalition controls 222 of the 393 seats in the elected House of Representatives.
The 1997/98 budget is scheduled to obtain final parliament approval by late September.
